research_rationale: Identity. The held Federal Register text (14 FR 289, issue of January 20, 1949, PDF page 1) is headed Executive Order 10029. It creates an emergency board under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act to investigate the dispute between Northwest Airlines, Inc. and certain of its employees represented by the International Association of Machinists, and it is signed by Harry S. Truman at The White House, January 19, 1949. The Civil Service Commission notices printed below the order on the same page are separate documents and are not part of the order. Inventory. The order is one block of text with four commands: create a three-member board, bar members from any interest in an employee organization or carrier, require the board to report within thirty days of the order, and forbid any change except by agreement in the conditions out of which the dispute arose from the order's date until thirty days after the board has made its report. I read the whole text; the verified one-clause inventory covers all of it and no operative sentence lies outside it. End. The last command to end is the no-change command, which by its own terms runs until thirty days after the board made its report. The report date comes from the dated letter of transmittal of Presidential Emergency Board report No. 67, held as PDF bytes (jobs/astra-source-retention/output/pdf/afc5c581e901d6a22180aebbd1dcba9cf853d1b4301b339fc05a647b158bbee9.pdf, SHA-256 verified) and cited here as a reviewed factual event. The letter is dated Casper, Wyoming, March 10, 1949 and says the board submits its report herewith; I read the page image, which shows March 10, 1949 (the text layer misreads the month). Thirty days after March 10, 1949 is April 9, 1949 (21 days remain in March after the 10th, and 9 more fall in April). I record the end as April 9, 1949, inclusive of that day, under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21; the exclusive reading, under which the command ends when April 9 begins, is the alternative. The letter date is the date of submission; receipt by the President may have been later, and no held source gives a receipt date. Recited events. The same letter recites that the President extended the board's time to report by thirty days by an order dated February 11, 1949. That order is not held, and it affects only when the report was due, not the thirty-day measure, which runs from the actual report; it is not claimed as an event. Later pages of the held report record that the parties settled the dispute by an agreement placed in the record, and that the chairman received the joint certificate of ratification on March 10, 1949. The no-change sentence permits changes by agreement, so the settlement is not a source that ended the sentence earlier; I found no held source showing an earlier end. Later events. Executive Order 12553 (signed February 25, 1986, 51 FR 7237, Federal Register of March 3, 1986) lists this order by number in a table of orders revoked together with any amendments to them; it came 37 years after the own-terms end and is recorded as the formal disposition. No amendment of this order is held. Searches. The U.S. Code search (release point through 2026-10-09), the eCFR search as of 2026-10-14 and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note search returned no other instrument affecting this order. Savings: none found.
savings_reason: Executive Order 12553, read in full, is one revoking sentence, a table of revoked orders, an editorial note and the date line, with no saving or transition provision. The commands of this order were a one-time board investigation and report and a standstill that expired by its own terms on 1949-04-09; no held source shows any appointment, transfer or right created under it that survived.
earlier_end_check: Searched the held texts for this order's number with the packet's bounded name search (one matching file, the order's own Federal Register text) and read the coverage notes of the three bounded machine searches. The only later instrument that names this order is Executive Order 12553, signed 1986-02-25, which revokes it. The Federal Register catalog disposition notes name only that order. No earlier revocation, supersession or amendment of this order is held. Under the owner ruling of 2026-10-28 the cleanup revocation is the formal disposition and not the first end. The first end is the order's own no-change term measured from the actual report date; a report deadline is not used as an end.
scope_check: The one clause covers the order's whole operative text, from the heading through the sentence that ends the standstill; the Civil Service Commission notices on the same page belong to other documents. Its commands are to create the board, to bar interested members, to report within thirty days of the order, and the no-change standstill. The standstill is the last of them to end, so the clause as a whole ended when the standstill ended on 1949-04-09.
independent_command_check: The report-within-thirty-days command is a deadline, not an end. The board's task was completed when it submitted its report; the dated transmittal letter evidences submission on 1949-03-10 (receipt by the President may have been later). The bar on interested members attaches to the board's membership, and no held source shows the board sitting after its report. The standstill is the only command with a continuing term of its own and it is measured from the report date. No command outlasts 1949-04-09.
savings_check: Nothing in the order creates an appointment, transfer or right that outlasts it: the board delivered its report and the standstill expired. Executive Order 12553 contains no saving or transition provision.
